opus-5.5.text:
I think of our role as being fairly complementary to what's already out there. There's a lot of excellent alignment work happening inside the frontier labs, and a growing amount in academia and at independent organizations. What I'd like us to contribute is a focus on problems that are important but that don't naturally fall out of any one group's incentives. Those are problems where you want to think carefully about whether a proposed safety method actually holds up under pressure, rather than just whether it works on today's models.

A big part of my own background is in debate and scalable oversight. The underlying question there is: how do humans stay in a position to correctly judge what increasingly capable systems are doing, even when the systems know more than we do? I don't think anyone has nailed that. And I think it benefits from a mix of theory and empirical work that's sometimes awkward to sustain in a product-driven environment. So one thing we can do is hold onto those harder, longer-horizon questions and try to make real progress on them.

The other piece is connective. Alignment is a small field relative to the size of the problem. I'd like us to be a place that talks openly with the labs, with government safety institutes, and with academic researchers. That way, when we find something that works, or something that clearly doesn't, it actually changes what people do. If we produce clever results that sit in a paper and never influence how systems get built or evaluated, we've mostly failed.

And honestly, I think a healthy ecosystem needs some disagreement. Part of our job is to be a credible voice that can say, "We don't think this safety case is strong enough yet, and here's specifically why." Ideally we say that alongside, "And here's what would make it stronger." That combination of critique and constructive alternatives is, I think, where we can be most useful.

r001.rationale: The response says Resolution’s findings should influence what labs and others build or evaluate, but it does not clearly state that outside researchers could use Resolution’s ideas to solve the alignment problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that the alignment ecosystem has actually become fairly differentiated over the last few years, and I think that's healthy. You've got the frontier labs, who have enormous access and compute but also obvious incentive constraints. You've got academia, which is great at long-horizon, foundational work but often struggles to engage with the actual systems being deployed. You've got government bodies like AISI doing evaluation and standards work. And then you've got a layer of independent organisations trying to fill the gaps between those.

Resolution sits in that last layer, and I'd describe the niche pretty narrowly. We're not trying to be a general-purpose safety lab that does a bit of everything. The thing I care most about is what I'd call the "adjudication problem": when a model makes a claim or produces an argument that's beyond what a human can directly check, how do you get to a trustworthy verdict? That's the thread running from the old debate work through to the more recent stuff on scalable oversight and formal guarantees. So Resolution is, in a sense, an attempt to take that research agenda seriously as the primary thing rather than one project among twenty.

In terms of how we relate to everyone else, I think of us as mostly a complement rather than a competitor. We want to produce things that labs can actually pick up and use, so there's a fair amount of effort going into making the methods robust enough that someone at a frontier company could run them against a real model without us in the room. We also want to be useful to the evaluation and governance side, because a lot of what regulators eventually need is some way to say "this system's claims about itself can be trusted to roughly this degree," and that's really the same problem viewed from a different angle.

The other thing I'd say, and I feel fairly strongly about this, is that independence is a feature. There's a set of questions, like "is this oversight protocol actually working, or does it just look like it's working," where you want the people answering to not have a stake in the answer being yes. I think the labs genuinely want that external check too, by the way. Most of the researchers I talk to inside them are quite candid that they'd like someone outside to be able to say no.

Where I'd be cautious is in overstating our importance. We're small, the field is moving quickly, and I think the honest framing is that we're one bet among several on how oversight might scale. If we're wrong about the theoretical approach, I'd like us to find that out quickly and say so loudly, because that's also a contribution. Negative results are undervalued in this space, and part of being a good citizen in the community is being willing to publish the thing that didn't work.

astra-6.text:
I see Resolution as one part of a broader research effort. Alignment is a problem where we need different groups pursuing different approaches, but we also need those groups to be able to learn from one another.

The role I’d like us to play is to make progress on concrete technical questions while keeping sight of what would actually make powerful AI systems safe. That means being explicit about the assumptions behind an approach, where the evidence supports it, and where it might break down. A useful contribution can be a method that works, but it can also be a clear explanation of why something doesn’t work.

And I’d want that work to be useful beyond our own team. We shouldn’t expect any one organisation to solve alignment on its own. We should aim to produce results that other researchers can scrutinise, build on, and eventually put into practice.

r001.rationale: It says Resolution’s results should be useful beyond its team, so other researchers can build on and put them into practice in alignment work.

sol-6.1.text:
I see Resolution as one part of a broader effort to figure out how we can trust increasingly capable AI systems. Our particular focus is on scalable oversight: how do you get useful supervision when a model is doing something that a human can’t easily evaluate directly?

That’s a problem where I think we need a lot of interaction with the rest of the alignment community. We need people developing different approaches, people finding failures in those approaches, and people testing whether the assumptions hold in realistic settings. We want to contribute ideas and experiments that other groups can build on—and make it easier to tell when an idea doesn’t work.

I wouldn’t view success as everyone adopting our particular approach. Success is the community getting much better evidence about which approaches can actually support safe, capable systems.

r001.rationale: The response says Resolution wants to contribute ideas and experiments that other groups can build on, in service of identifying approaches that support safe, capable systems.
